        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) whenever you push to `main`.  

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone, commit or push the repo from here, but the instructions below will get you up and running in minutes.

---

## 1. Clone the repo (local copy)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Add the new files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Node.js 18 (Alpine for small size)
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies (production only)
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *If your app listens on a different port, change `EXPOSE 3000` and the CMD accordingly.*

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and add `deployment.yaml` inside it:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- will be built by GitHub Actions
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> *If you prefer a different service type (e.g., `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`), change `type:` accordingly.*

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GHCR
      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> *The workflow uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate with GHCR. No extra secrets are required.*

---

## 3. Commit & Push the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to GHCR. You can then deploy the Kubernetes manifests to any cluster that has access to GHCR (or you can add a `docker pull` step in your deployment pipeline).

---

## 4. Verify

1. **Check the Actions tab** – you should see a successful run for “Build & Push Docker Image”.
2. **Verify the image** – run `docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` locally to confirm it pulls correctly.
3. **Deploy to Kubernetes** – apply the manifest:

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

   Then expose the service (if you’re using `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`, adjust the manifest accordingly).

---

### Quick Recap

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas and exposes a service |
| `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

That’s it! Your repo now contains everything needed for containerization, Kubernetes deployment, and automated CI/CD. Happy coding!
